young valley: A valley that is in its earliest stages of de- velopment. Such a valley is usually V-shaped in cross section, with a narrow bottom, relatively steep slopes, and poorly developed small tributaries. See also youthful valley.
youthful valley: A stream valley that is still in the early stages of its development. Such a valley is usually V-shaped in cross section, has a narrow bot- tom with a steep gradient, has few tributaries, and is of relatively short length.
yr: See year in the Units of Measure section. reservoir or impoundment, the yield per foot (meter) is the volume of water produced for each foot (meter) of decline in storage depth. See also circle of influ- ence; cone of depression; drawdown; specific capacity; zone of influence.
yoke: (1) A designed meter setter providing proper spacing, alignment, and bracing of the inlet and out- let pipes, allowing simplified setting and removal of meters. (2) A 45° branch in the shape of a letter Y.
young professional (YP): Term used to describe peo- ple just starting their careers, typically 35 years old or younger.
young river: In geological terms, a river that is actively eroding its channel. A B C D E F Y H I Copyright (C) 2010 American Water Works Association All Rights Reserved A Z
z coordinate: The third element of a point's location in space in a Cartesian coordinate system. The horizon- tal positions are identified by x and y coordinates. The z coordinate identifies the vertical position, or eleva- tion, of a point or feature. See also x–y coordinates.
zebra mussel: A bivalve that has become a serious pest because it blocks intake pipes. See also Dreissena polymorpha; quagga mussel.
Zeeman background correction: An instrumental technique of compensating for interferences in graph- ite furnace atomic absorption spectrophotometry. In this technique, a strong magnetic field divides spectral lines into polarized components. Background correc- tors based on the Zeeman effect are independent of the analyte and wavelength used in the determination.
zeolite: Any of numerous hydrated sodium alumina silicates, either naturally occurring mined products or synthetic products, with ion-exchange properties. Zeolites were formerly used extensively for residen- tial and commercial water softening but have been largely replaced by synthetic organic cation resin ion exchangers. Modified zeolites, such as manganese greensand and synthetic manganese zeolites, are still used as catalyst/oxidizing filter media for the re- moval of iron, hydrogen sulfide, and manganese. See also cation-exchange resin; manganese greensand; manganese zeolite.
zeolite filter: In water softening, a treatment unit de- signed to remove certain chemical constituents from water by base exchange. Zeolite is the exchange me- dium. See also zeolite process.
zeolite process: A process of softening water by pass- ing it through a zeolite substance that exchanges other constituents for hardness constituents in the water.
zeolite softening: The removal of calcium and magne- sium hardness from water by a base-exchange pro- cess using natural or synthetic zeolites. Since the introduction of synthetic organic cation-exchange resins, zeolite softening has generally been replaced by cation-exchange softening. Zeolite softening was also called base exchange. See also cation exchange.
zero-base budget: A system of budgeting in which re- source allocations, from zero to the top, are deter- mined within the total budget in terms of achieving organization objectives, with opportunities and risks taken into account. A process in finance justifying an overall budget each fiscal year or review period rather than dealing only with proposed changes from a previous budget.
zero-coupon bond: A bond purchased at a large dis- count relative to its value at maturity. The bond then earns interest that is reinvested, helping the bond grow to its stated value at maturity. For example, a 5-year $1,000 zero-coupon bond earning interest of 8.0 percent per year would be initially sold for $680.58 and redeemed 5 years later for $1,000. The retention of interest makes a zero-coupon bond a powerful earning instrument. Although the interest is not paid out to the bondholders as it is earned, it is taxable in the year it is earned. A zero-coupon bond is also called a capital-appreciation bond. See also deep-discount bond.
zero discharge: Term used to describe the operation of a facility that results in no discharge to a body of wa- ter. In water treatment, this commonly means the re- cycle of all liquid streams and the disposal of solids on land. Land spraying of liquids or use as irrigation water would similarly be considered to be zero dis- charge if the material does not reach a water body. Discharge to a wastewater plant would not be zero discharge as the effluent of the wastewater plant gen- erally is discharged to a water body.
zero-moisture index: The amount of precipitation uni- formly distributed throughout the year that would supply all the water needed for maximum evapora- tion and transpiration. Annual precipitation in excess of the zero-moisture index will produce surface run- off and recharge to the groundwater system. Annual precipitation less than the zero-moisture index will require moisture stored in the soil to be used to sat- isfy the evaporation–transpiration requirement. The zero-moisture index is so called because annual pre- cipitation at this value would not change the soil moisture content during the year.
zero point of charge (ZPC): The pH corresponding to a surface charge of zero on a particle. Many particles found in natural waters have surface charges depen- dent on the solution pH and can exhibit both positive and negative charges (i.e., can be amphoteric). See also electrokinetic potential; electrophoretic mobil- ity; streaming current.
zero soft water: Water produced by the cation-exchange process and having less than 1.0 grain per gallon (17.1 milligrams per liter) as calcium carbonate (CaCO3).

zone of aeration: The soil or rock located between the ground surface and the top of the water table.
zone of coagulation: Term used to describe one of the four conditions for particulate removal by coagula- tion based on the initial solids concentration of the water and the coagulant dose. The four zones are typ- ically shown graphically where the residual turbidity is plotted as a function of coagulant dose. In zone 1, insufficient coagulant is present to allow destabiliza- tion of the particles. As the concentration of the posi- tively charged coagulant is increased, the negatively charged particles are neutralized, and they tend to ag- glomerate. This zone of coagulation, zone 2, is called the destabilization by charge neutralization zone. As the concentration of the positively charged coagulant is increased further, however, the particles may be- come positively charged and again resist agglomera- tion. This is called the restabilization zone, or zone 3. Finally, at high concentrations of the coagulant, the particles may become enmeshed in the chemical pre- cipitate formed by the coagulant. This zone, zone 4, is called the sweep coagulation zone or the sweep floc zone. See also coagulant, coagulation.
zone of influence: The area around a well or well field that experiences a measurable drawdown during pump- ing of the well or group of wells. See also circle of in- fluence; cone of depression; drawdown; well cone of influence.
zone of saturation: That part of an aquifer that has all available pore spaces filled with water.
zoning: A civil process that specifies which types of land use are allowable in specific locations.
zoonosis: An infection or disease transmissible under natural conditions from vertebrate animals to humans.
zooplankton: Microscopic animals living unattached in aquatic ecosystems. They include single-celled an- imals and small crustacea.
zoospore: An asexual spore produced by certain algae and some fungi. See also spore.
zwitterion: A molecule in which the positive and nega- tive groups are equally ionized. At the isoelectric point—the pH at which the net charge of a molecule in solution is zero—amino acids exist almost en- tirely in the zwitterion state. In the zwitterion struc- ture of an amino acid, the acidic proton from the carboxyl group has been appropriated by the basic ni- trogen of the amino group. See also amino acid; iso- electric point; zero point of charge.

zeta potential (: ζ) An operationally determined mea- sure of the charge of a particle. According to Gouy- Chapman theory, the distribution of charge in the vi- cinity of a charged particle can be thought of in terms of an electric double layer. One layer is seen as fixed to the particle surface, while the other is distributed in the liquid around the particle. When the particle moves through the liquid, the fixed layer of charge moves with the particle, while the outer layer remains stationary. The interface between these two layers is referred to as the shear plane. Note that the distance between the actual particle surface and the shear plane cannot be accurately measured. Zeta potential is theoretically defined as the difference in electric potential at this shear plane and the bulk liquid. Oper- ationally, zeta potential (ζ) can be calculated from electrophoretic mobility measurements, in which the velocity of a particle subjected to a known electric field is measured. zeta potential meter: A device used to measure the zeta potential of a water sample. This type of meter is used to control the dosage of coagulants in water treatment and is also called an electrophoretic mobil- ity apparatus.
zinc (Zn): A metallic element that is an essential growth element in terms of nutrition. Zinc is used industrially in alloys, electroplating, batteries, and fungicides. See also fungicide; zinc orthophosphate.
zinc orthophosphate (Zn: 3(PO4)2) A chemical used in corrosion control that reacts with the surface of a pipe to form a protective coating. See also corrosion; corrosion inhibitor.
